sections.normalized_html:
Theorem (DAG criterion): A directed graph is a directed acyclic graph if and only if it has a topological ordering.

Proof:

DAG [MATH: \Rightarrow] TO. This direction is proven using Kahn's Algorithm, which will be discussed in a future topic. The algorithm provides a procedure for constructing a topological ordering for any DAG.

DAG [MATH: \Leftarrow] TO. This direction can be proven by contradiction:

Suppose a topological ordering (TO) exists, but the graph is not a DAG and contains a cycle.

Since the TO exists, it includes all vertices of this cycle. Let [MATH: v] be the first vertex of the cycle in the ordering. By the definition of a cycle, there must be an incoming edge to [MATH: v] from another vertex [MATH: u] within the cycle.

However, because this is a topological ordering, [MATH: u] must appear earlier than [MATH: v] in the ordering. This contradicts the assumption that [MATH: v] is the first vertex of the cycle in the ordering.

This contradiction implies that our initial assumption is false, and therefore, the graph must be a DAG.

items.readable_text:
Content:
A topological ordering (TO, or topological sort) of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge [MATH: u \to v] from vertex [MATH: u] to vertex [MATH: v], [MATH: u] appears before [MATH: v] in the ordering.

Content:
Alternatively, a topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that, if we arrange the vertices in order from left to right, each vertex has all its successors positioned to the right and all its predecessors to the left. Equivalently, all edges point from left to right.

Content:
For example, consider the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2739d4a5f12ec1ca6c4cbffc25f671cb]

Content:
To obtain a topological ordering, the vertices of this graph can be rearranged as follows: [MATH: v_1, v_2, v_4, v_5, v_3.] The image below illustrates this topological ordering.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/25290950e0de7de42134302edbe83889]

Content:
Note:

Content:
- A topological ordering is not a new graph but a different visual representation of the same graph.
- Topological orderings are not unique. Graphs usually have multiple topological orderings. For example, a graph with [MATH: n] isolated vertices has [MATH: n!] topological orderings since its vertices can be arranged in any order.

Recall that a topological ordering (TO) of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge [MATH: u \to v] from vertex [MATH: u] to vertex [MATH: v], [MATH: u] appears before [MATH: v] in the ordering.

Alternatively, we can say that in a topological ordering, each vertex must have all its successors positioned to the right and all its predecessors to the left.

Notice that the missing vertices are [MATH: v_2, v_3,] and [MATH: v_5,] and they should be ordered relative to each other.

By inspecting the graph, we can observe the following dependencies:

  • The vertex [MATH: v_5] has no successors. Hence, it is the rightmost vertex: [MATH: \square, \: v_4, \: \: \square, \: v_1, \: v_6, \bbox[3pt,Moccasin]{v_5}]

  • The vertex [MATH: v_2] has no predecessors. Hence, it is the leftmost vertex: [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Moccasin]{v_2}, \: v_4,\: \: \square, \: v_1, \: v_6, \: v_5]

  • The vertex [MATH: v_1] is successor of [MATH: v_3.] Hence, [MATH: v_3] must be positioned to the left of [MATH: v_1{:}] [MATH: v_2, \: v_4, \: \bbox[3pt,Moccasin]{v_3}, \: v_1, \: v_6, \: v_5]

The corresponding layout of the DAG representing this topological ordering is shown below.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A topological ordering (TO, or topological sort) of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every directed edge [MATH: u \to v] from vertex [MATH: u] to vertex [MATH: v], [MATH: u] appears before [MATH: v] in the ordering.

Content:
Alternatively, a topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that, if we arrange the vertices in order from left to right, each vertex has all its successors positioned to the right and all its predecessors to the left. Equivalently, all edges point from left to right.

Content:
For example, consider the graph below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2739d4a5f12ec1ca6c4cbffc25f671cb]

Content:
To obtain a topological ordering, the vertices of this graph can be rearranged as follows: [MATH: v_1, v_2, v_4, v_5, v_3.] The image below illustrates this topological ordering.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/25290950e0de7de42134302edbe83889]

Content:
Note:

Content:
- A topological ordering is not a new graph but a different visual representation of the same graph.
- Topological orderings are not unique. Graphs usually have multiple topological orderings. For example, a graph with [MATH: n] isolated vertices has [MATH: n!] topological orderings since its vertices can be arranged in any order.

Content:
For another example, both images below represent valid topological orderings of the graph above.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/fb4d72ffb2d500291b0beeeac3553147]

Content:
Notice that the two weakly connected components of the initial graph remain disconnected from each other in the topological orderings.

Content:
We have the following theorem:

Content:
> Theorem (DAG criterion): A directed graph is a directed acyclic graph if and only if it has a topological ordering.
>
> Proof:
>
> DAG [MATH: \Rightarrow] TO. This direction is proven using Kahn's Algorithm, which will be discussed in a future topic. The algorithm provides a procedure for constructing a topological ordering for any DAG.
>
> DAG [MATH: \Leftarrow] TO. This direction can be proven by contradiction:
>
> Suppose a topological ordering (TO) exists, but the graph is not a DAG and contains a cycle.
>
> Since the TO exists, it includes all vertices of this cycle. Let [MATH: v] be the first vertex of the cycle in the ordering. By the definition of a cycle, there must be an incoming edge to [MATH: v] from another vertex [MATH: u] within the cycle.
>
> However, because this is a topological ordering, [MATH: u] must appear earlier than [MATH: v] in the ordering. This contradicts the assumption that [MATH: v] is the first vertex of the cycle in the ordering.
>
> This contradiction implies that our initial assumption is false, and therefore, the graph must be a DAG.

---

Content:
1. [MATH: v_3, v_2, v_1, v_4, v_5]
2. [MATH: v_3, v_2, v_4, v_1, v_5]
3. [MATH: v_3, v_1, v_2, v_4, v_5]

Content:
With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

Content:
- Option I is a topological ordering because all edges are directed from a preceding vertex to a succeeding vertex in this list. The corresponding layout of the DAG representing this topological ordering is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d8e07d8dfaa5c5cf46b52b1c810d8e24]

Content:
- Option II is a topological ordering because all edges are directed from a preceding vertex to a succeeding vertex in this list. The corresponding layout of the DAG representing this topological ordering is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7f626367f2eda7d5cc94eff898e867f1]

Content:
- Option III is not a topological ordering because [MATH: v_2] succeeds [MATH: v_1,] but our DAG contains the edge [MATH: v_2 \to v_1] (opposite direction).

Content:
Therefore, only options I and II represent topological orderings for the graph.
